A few additional thoughts after months of refining this direction that may help:

The biggest realization is that the signature of the brand is no longer just the accent over the É—it's the entire **V language**.

The larger opening V should be the hero of the wordmark. The smaller closing V and the É accent should all be derived from that same geometry. Together, these three elements should share identical angles, proportions, and material language. Ideally, if someone covered every other letter except the two Vs and the accent, it should still feel unmistakably like VELLVÉ.

The remaining letters should support the V rather than compete with it. The strongest direction we found was treating them as architectural objects instead of typography—quiet, sculptural, and intentional.

Some additional refinements I'd love to explore are:

• Perfecting the kerning so the word reads as one unified mark rather than "VE LL VÉ."
• Making the Ls feel more structural than typographic. We gravitated toward taller, architectural proportions with subtle custom geometry rather than decorative serifs.
• Refining the É accent so it feels like a brand signature rather than punctuation—slightly shorter, thicker, and more integrated with the V geometry.
• Exploring subtle internal reveal lines or dimensional details that create depth without feeling ornamental. The logo should feel like it could exist as a beautifully crafted brass or stone sign, where light naturally catches the details.

One important realization was that the logo became too severe when we leaned too heavily into architecture. I still want it to feel timeless and sculptural, but with a sense of warmth, vitality, and aspiration. We found that warmth came from the material expression—champagne metal, light, subtle illumination, and depth—not from softer or more decorative typography.

Please feel free to challenge the typography, but preserve the design language. I'm more interested in refining the DNA of the wordmark than introducing entirely new ideas.

Ultimately, I don't think this project is about creating a beautiful font. It's about creating a proprietary wordmark that feels inevitable—as though VELLVÉ could never have been written any other way.

If there's one thing I'd love to achieve, it's this: the opening V should eventually become recognizable enough to stand on its own as a long-term brand asset, without ever needing a separate icon or monogram. The wordmark itself should become the identity.

value_updates.hero_role: larger opening V and primary wordmark anchor
value_updates.geometry_role: master geometry for the V system

Hi Abdulbari,

Thank you for continuing to explore this. I do think this represents an important shift in thinking. I appreciate that you've moved beyond designing the right arm in isolation and are now considering the relationship between the two arms. I think that's absolutely the right direction.

That said, I don't think we've discovered the design language of this V yet.

Rather than continuing to refine one family of ideas, I'd actually love to zoom back out again and see a broader range of concepts before we begin narrowing in on a final direction.

Instead of multiple refinements of one construction, I'd love to see several fundamentally different ways of thinking about the letter. For example, you might explore ideas like:

a V that is almost impossibly restrained
a V that feels subtly sculptural
a V inspired by the precision of stone carving
a V inspired by the elegance of an architectural cantilever
a V that achieves distinction through optical balance rather than geometry
a V that creates tension through proportion instead of overlap
a V whose asymmetry is almost invisible until you study it

These aren't intended as requirements. They're simply different creative philosophies that might reveal something unexpected.

I also don't want the exploration to become only about the vertex. I think the identity of this V will come from designing three things simultaneously:

the quiet stability of the left arm
the unique expression of the right arm
the relationship where the two resolve at the vertex

I don't think those can be solved independently.

As you continue exploring, I'm less interested in geometric cleverness and more interested in how the letter feels.

I'm looking for a V that feels:

elegant
confident
quietly expressive
sculptural
intentional
architecturally resolved
visually balanced
never bulky
never gimmicky
never attention-seeking

Most importantly, I want the right arm to contribute character without becoming the character. The viewer should experience a beautiful V first, and only later discover why it feels different.

I'm attaching the concept board again because I think it still communicates the emotional direction better than words alone. I don't want you to recreate those exact shapes, but I do think they capture the feeling I'm after: refined, architectural, elevated, and harmonious. They don't feel like "a normal V plus a special right arm." They simply feel like one beautifully resolved letter.

The sentence that continues to resonate most with me is:

"Design a V whose asymmetry disappears because the composition is so beautifully resolved."

I think that's the north star. I'm not looking to optimize this particular V—I think we're still discovering it. I'm excited to see several fresh directions before we begin refining one.
